body:
Why land revenue mattered

Land revenue was the principal source of income for the Mughal state. Revenue officials needed information about cultivated land, crops, agricultural output and the amount that could be demanded from cultivators.

The Mughal fiscal administration included the diwan, who supervised financial and revenue matters, along with officials responsible for measurement, assessment, records and collection.

Assessment and collection were different stages

Two Persian terms are essential:

  • Jama: The land-revenue demand assessed or fixed by the administration.
  • Hasil: The revenue actually collected.

An assessment of a particular amount did not guarantee that the entire amount would be recovered. Crop failures, local resistance, administrative difficulties and other conditions could produce a difference between jama and hasil.

Akbar's revenue arrangements

Akbar's administration sought to make revenue assessment more systematic. His revenue minister Raja Todar Mal is closely associated with these reforms.

Under the zabt system, land was measured and crop-wise revenue rates were fixed using information about agricultural production and prices. The dahsala arrangement used averages based on records covering approximately 10 years. These averages helped establish revenue demands, often expressed in money.

The system required reliable information about fields and crops. Consequently, it could not be applied with equal effectiveness across all regions of the empire. Areas with difficult geographical conditions, different patterns of cultivation or insufficient measurement records continued to use other methods.

The association of Akbar and Todar Mal with a systematic revenue arrangement does not mean that every Mughal village paid one identical rate or that revenue was collected everywhere by the same method.

Classification of agricultural land

Akbar's administration distinguished several categories of land according to the continuity of cultivation and the length of time for which a field had remained fallow.

Land categoryMeaningIdentifying feature
PolajLand cultivated regularly.Continually cultivated without being left fallow.
ParautiLand temporarily left uncultivated.Rested for a period to recover fertility.
ChacharLand remaining fallow for 3–4 years.A longer period without cultivation.
BanjarLand remaining uncultivated for 5 years or more.The longest fallow category in this classification.

The distinction is based on the history of cultivation, not simply on whether land is fertile or infertile. In particular, parauti land was deliberately rested and could return to cultivation.

Methods of determining and collecting revenue

The Mughal system allowed different methods of estimating agricultural output and dividing or collecting the state's share.

  • Kankut: Estimation of the crop and its expected produce.
  • Batai or bhaoli: Division of the harvested produce between the parties according to an agreed share.
  • Khet-batai: Division of the fields after sowing.
  • Lang-batai: Division of harvested produce after it had been collected into heaps.

Although the state often preferred payment in cash, payment in kind was also possible. The Ain-i Akbari records these different practices. The share claimed by the state varied with the arrangement and circumstances; it should not be assumed that every peasant always surrendered exactly the same fraction of actual output.

The connection with the wider economy

Where revenue was assessed and paid in money, cultivators needed access to cash. Selling crops or producing goods for markets could help them meet these demands. Consequently, land-revenue arrangements encouraged connections between cultivation, money and trade.

Prelims focus

  • Jama: assessed revenue; hasil: revenue actually collected.
  • Raja Todar Mal is associated with Akbar's revenue reforms.
  • Dahsala used averages covering approximately 10 years.
  • Polaj: regularly cultivated; parauti: temporarily fallow.
  • Chachar: fallow for 3–4 years; banjar: uncultivated for 5 years or more.
  • Trap: Batai involved sharing produce; it was not the same as assigning a jagir to an officer.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Theme 8, Peasants, Zamindars and the State, printed pp. 213–215, section 6, Land Revenue System; NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Chapter 4, The Mughal Empire, section on Akbar's revenue administration.]

pictures.caption: Jama and hasil represented different stages.

title: Mughal Land Revenue: Assessment, Collection and Land Classification

body:
Crafts in the Mughal economy

The Mughal economy supported a wide range of crafts. Agricultural households produced raw materials such as cotton, while skilled artisans converted those materials into textiles, clothing, ornaments, tools and household goods.

Craft production occurred in both villages and towns. Many rural households combined farming with seasonal craft work. Urban centres, however, often supported greater specialisation and production for distant markets.

Major crafts and their products

  • Textiles: Cotton cloth, fine muslin, silk fabrics, dyeing, embroidery and decorative weaving.
  • Metalworking: Agricultural implements, weapons, armour, utensils and jewellery.
  • Stonework: Architectural carving, decorative screens, tombs, palaces and other buildings.
  • Carpets and furnishings: Woven carpets, embroidered fabrics and luxury objects for wealthy households.
  • Manuscript crafts: Paper preparation, calligraphy, painting, gilding and bookbinding.

Different regions developed particular specialisations. Bengal was associated with fine cotton textiles, while Gujarat was an important centre for textile manufacture and trade. Kashmir was known for shawls and other luxury crafts.

Karkhanas and imperial patronage

The Mughals maintained royal workshops called karkhanas. These produced or supplied goods required by the imperial household, court and administration.

Workers could manufacture fine clothing, weapons, jewellery, carpets, furnishings and other specialised products. The ruler and nobility provided important demand for skilled artisans.

Akbar took an active interest in the work of craftsmen and painters. Skilled workers could receive recognition and rewards. Mughal artistic production therefore depended heavily on local craftsmanship, even when designs incorporated Persian or Central Asian influences.

A karkhana was a royal or organised workshop of the period. It should not automatically be understood as a modern mechanised factory.

How specialised textile production worked

Textile manufacture involved several activities rather than a single occupation. Cultivators produced cotton, workers prepared and spun fibres, weavers made cloth, and dyers, printers or embroiderers finished the fabric. Merchants then supplied local consumers or transported the cloth to distant markets.

The resulting product could range from inexpensive everyday cloth to costly fabrics commissioned by wealthy patrons.

Towns and urban functions

Mughal towns served different purposes, often combining several activities.

  • Agra, Delhi and Lahore: Major political, administrative and commercial centres.
  • Ahmedabad: An important Gujarat centre associated with textile production and commerce.
  • Surat: A major port connecting inland production with overseas trade.
  • Other market towns: Places where agricultural produce, craft goods and services were exchanged.

A town's economic importance might arise from its court, its market, its crafts or its location on a trade route. These categories could overlap. For example, an imperial centre attracted merchants and craftsmen because the court, officials and soldiers required goods and services.

Craft production and social mobility

Artisans were not socially equal. Their income and status depended on their occupation, patrons, skill and access to markets. Highly valued court painters and specialist craftsmen might receive considerable recognition, while ordinary workers faced more difficult conditions.

Changes in political patronage also affected artisans. As Mughal authority weakened in the 18th century, some skilled workers sought employment with regional rulers and other wealthy patrons. This helped carry artistic techniques into additional courts and towns.

Prelims focus

  • Karkhana: a royal or organised workshop.
  • Textile production included spinning, weaving, dyeing, printing and embroidery.
  • Agra, Delhi and Lahore combined political and commercial functions.
  • Ahmedabad and Surat were significant Gujarat centres of production and trade.
  • Imperial patronage supported luxury crafts and manuscript production.
  • Trap: Craft production was not confined to urban centres; villages also contained artisans.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Chapter 6, Towns, Traders and Craftspersons, printed pp. 75–90; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Theme 8, printed pp. 204–206; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Chapter Crafts in the Past, sections on karkhanas and craft patronage.]

title: Craft Production, Imperial Workshops and Mughal Towns

body:
Trade connected villages, towns and ports

The Mughal Empire participated in extensive inland and overseas trade. Agricultural produce and manufactured goods moved between villages, market towns, major cities and ports. Merchants also imported goods that were not produced locally or were especially valued by wealthy buyers.

Trade routes included roads, river transport and sea routes. Caravans carried goods overland, while boats and ships moved goods along navigable waterways and across the seas.

Inland trade and merchant communities

Merchants purchased crops, textiles and other products from producers and supplied them to consumers elsewhere. Grain traders and transporting groups, including the Banjaras, played important roles in moving provisions and other commodities.

Overland commerce also connected India with Central Asia and Afghanistan through centres such as Kabul. Horses were an important item of this wider trade.

Markets, credit and money exchange

Trade required more than physical transportation. Merchants needed credit, reliable payments and ways to transfer money between distant places.

A hundi was a financial instrument used to facilitate payment or remittance. It could help a merchant conduct transactions without carrying the entire value of a purchase in coins over a long distance.

Shroffs were money changers and financial intermediaries. They exchanged currencies and could assist commercial transactions.

A sarai was an establishment providing temporary accommodation to travellers, merchants or other people using trade routes. Sarais supported movement and interaction rather than manufacturing goods.

Surat: Gujarat's major Mughal-period port

Surat, on the western coast of Gujarat, was one of the most important commercial ports of Mughal India. It served as a gateway for trade with West Asia through the Persian Gulf and Red Sea routes.

Surat was also associated with ships carrying pilgrims towards the Islamic holy places. This connection contributed to its reputation as a gateway to Mecca.

Portuguese, Dutch and English trading companies maintained commercial establishments and warehouses at Surat. In this context, the word factory usually referred to a trading station operated by company agents, not a modern industrial plant.

Major exports and commercial services

Textiles were among the important goods traded through Surat. Gujarat's cotton fabrics, including decorative textiles and cloth associated with gold-thread work, reached distant markets.

Surat also had active merchant and banking communities. Financial instruments such as hundis helped link its commercial activity with other Indian and overseas centres.

Khambat and Ahmedabad

Khambat, historically called Cambay, was another important Gujarat port with longstanding connections to maritime commerce.

Ahmedabad was a major inland centre of manufacturing and trade. Commercial networks linked such production centres with ports, allowing textiles and other goods to reach overseas buyers.

These locations had different primary functions: Ahmedabad was an important inland commercial centre, while Surat and Khambat were maritime outlets. Their economic activities nevertheless reinforced one another.

Oceanic trade and the flow of silver

Indian textiles and other goods were purchased by merchants dealing with West Asia, Southeast Asia and Europe. The expansion of overseas trade brought considerable quantities of silver into India because foreign buyers often paid for Indian merchandise with precious metal.

Silver contributed to the circulation of the rupya, the silver coin used in the Mughal monetary system. Wider availability of money assisted trade and made cash revenue payments more feasible.

It is important to distinguish the direction of flows: manufactured goods were exported from India, while a substantial part of the payment for those goods entered India as silver bullion.

Prelims focus

  • Surat was a major Mughal-period port on the western coast of Gujarat.
  • Khambat was historically known as Cambay.
  • Ahmedabad was an important inland manufacturing and commercial centre.
  • Hundi: financial instrument for payment or remittance.
  • Shroff: money changer or financial intermediary.
  • Trap: A European company factory at Surat was primarily a trading establishment, not necessarily an industrial factory.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Chapter 6, Towns, Traders and Craftspersons, printed pp. 75–90, especially the section A Gateway to the West: Surat; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Theme 8, printed pp. 205–206 and 215–217, section The Flow of Silver.]

title: Inland and Overseas Trade: The Importance of Surat and Gujarat

body:
Meaning and characteristics of Mughal miniature painting

Mughal miniature painting was a refined tradition of small-scale painting that developed in the imperial workshops from the 16th century. Many paintings illustrated handwritten books, while others were made as independent portraits or collected in albums.

Artists combined techniques associated with Persian manuscript painting with Indian subjects, artistic practices and the skills of local painters. European pictures later contributed additional visual elements.

Mughal painting frequently depicted court ceremonies, battles, royal processions, hunting expeditions, portraits, animals, birds, plants and episodes from literary works.

Babur and Humayun: the foundations

Babur, the founder of the Mughal Empire in India, possessed a strong interest in nature, literature and artistic accomplishments. His memoirs record observations about people, landscapes and plants.

The development of an organised imperial painting workshop gained momentum under Humayun. During his exile, Humayun encountered the sophisticated painting traditions of the Safavid court in Iran.

He invited 2 important Persian painters to work for him:

  • Mir Sayyid Ali
  • Abd us Samad

Their artistic experience helped establish a court painting tradition that expanded greatly under Humayun's successor, Akbar.

Akbar and the imperial painting workshop

During Akbar's reign, the imperial workshop developed into a major centre of manuscript illustration. Artists of different backgrounds worked together. Persian painters contributed established techniques, while Indian artists introduced local styles, subjects and methods of depicting people and landscapes.

Paintings were often produced collaboratively. One artist might prepare the composition, another might colour major forms, and another might complete faces or fine details. Akbar took a personal interest in the work and recognised accomplished painters.

Major illustrated manuscripts

Hamzanama

The Hamzanama was an important early illustrated manuscript project associated with Humayun's artistic legacy and expanded under Akbar. Its paintings illustrated adventurous narratives about Amir Hamza. It is particularly associated with large, dynamic and colourful compositions.

Razmnama

The Razmnama, meaning Book of Wars, was the Persian translation of the Sanskrit Mahabharata undertaken during Akbar's reign. Its illustrated manuscripts demonstrate the interest of the Mughal court in Indian literary traditions.

Akbarnama

The Akbarnama, written by Abu'l Fazl, recorded Akbar's reign and was illustrated with paintings of political events, battles, court scenes and other activities. It combined written history with visual representation.

Important artists of Akbar's reign

  • Daswant or Daswanth: A prominent Indian artist associated with Akbar's workshop and important illustrated manuscript projects.
  • Basawan: Known for accomplished composition, modelling of figures and the depiction of complex scenes.
  • Miskin: An important painter associated with animal and figure studies and narrative illustrations.

These artists worked within a large court tradition. A particular manuscript could involve numerous painters, so the existence of a celebrated artist does not mean that every painting in that manuscript was made by that person alone.

What made the new style distinctive?

Mughal painting increasingly combined fine line work, detailed observation, varied colours and more convincing representations of people and space. It did not simply reproduce Persian painting unchanged, nor did it replace all existing Indian traditions.

Akbar's workshop is especially associated with large illustrated manuscript projects. This emphasis helps distinguish his patronage from Jahangir's later preference for individual paintings, natural studies and albums.

Prelims focus

  • Humayun invited Mir Sayyid Ali and Abd us Samad.
  • Akbar expanded and organised imperial manuscript painting.
  • Hamzanama: an illustrated narrative associated with the early Mughal workshop.
  • Razmnama: Persian translation of the Mahabharata.
  • Akbarnama: illustrated chronicle of Akbar's reign.
  • Trap: Razmnama and Akbarnama were different works with different subject matter.

[Sources: NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part II, Chapter 3, The Mughal School of Miniature Painting, sections Influences on Mughal Painting, Early Mughal Painting and Akbar's patronage, consulted through SATHEE, IIT Kanpur, 19 November 2026; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part II, Theme 9, Kings and Chronicles, printed pp. 227–231.]
